problem: Zero-shot VLN/object-search systems either use lightweight reasoning (CLIP/detectors) that misses complex instructions, or call LLMs/VLMs every step, which is too slow for onboard deployment. Existing fast-slow designs are tightly coupled (the slow module blocks the fast one), give the slow module only fragmentary memory, and use greedy frontier selection that causes redundant exploration.
motivation: Real robots must react to local geometry at high frequency while also doing long-horizon semantic reasoning on tightly budgeted embedded compute. Fast action and slow reasoning work at different time scales, so they should run asynchronously and exchange information through a shared global memory rather than trigger each other. Frontier selection should also account for the spatial distribution of candidates and time-to-discovery, not just the single best score.
key_idea: Run a fast perception-action layer and a slow VLM reasoning layer asynchronously over a shared compact ILP-pruned cognitive memory graph (fed to the VLM as progressive subgraphs), and select exploration frontiers by solving a Weighted Traveling Repairman Problem.
insight: Decoupling VLM reasoning from control gives strong reasoning without blocking execution: the online variant finishes tasks in 21.5 s versus 298-569 s for the per-step-VLM baselines UniGoal and SG-Nav. In the TextNav ablation, replacing WTRP with greedy selection causes the largest drop (SR 27.8 to 25.4, SPL 12.9 to 11.8), while removing S_struct or S_vis costs about 1-1.3 SR points each, so global ordering matters more than the individual utility cues. Failure analysis shows cross-floor targets (13.9% MP3D, 18.5% HM3D) and false positives are the main remaining errors.
method: Three-layer asynchronous architecture: a real-time perception-action layer (SLAM localization, YOLO-World detection, obstacle avoidance, global/local planning), a memory construction layer, and a deep reasoning thread, all communicating through a shared memory.

Cognitive Memory Graph (CMG): a bipartite graph of visual anchors (keyframes chosen when a new object appears or the pose moves beyond a translation/rotation threshold) and object nodes (Mobile-SAM point cloud + CLIP feature), merged by a 3D IoU + CLIP similarity score.

ILP graph pruning: choose a minimal-cost subset of anchors such that each object is covered by at least r_j anchors (a weighted set multicover problem), keeping semantic completeness while compacting memory.

Subgraph decomposition and VLM reasoning: the VLM first splits the instruction into target objects O_t and related objects O_r. Subgraphs are built around these objects (plus per-anchor subgraphs for the rest) and ordered by CLIP-based priority. A separate thread queries Qwen3-Omni (API) or Qwen3-VL-8B (local) to judge target visibility, pick the anchor, and localize the target with a bounding box.

Context-aware frontier utility: S = λ1·S_struct + λ2·S_vis. S_struct sums Gaussian semantic fields of CMG objects, with a gain γ on the VLM-predicted related objects. S_vis is the CLIP similarity between the frontier's associated anchor image and the task.

WTRP goal selection: frontier utility is min-max normalized and exponentiated into weights. Transition cost is time-based (max of distance/v_max and heading change/ω_max), plus a motion-consistency term and a local-openness term for the first hop. The problem is solved with LKH and the first frontier in the sequence becomes the goal.
Planning and control: A* for distant goals or direct local planning for near ones, followed by trajectory optimization for collision-free velocity commands.

setting.backbone: Qwen3-Omni (API, frozen) or Qwen3-VL-8B (local, frozen) as the VLM; YOLO-World, Mobile-SAM, CLIP used off-the-shelf
setting.model_size: Qwen3-VL-8B for the offline variant; Qwen3-Omni is an API model (size not stated)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D (RealSense D455 on the real robot) + LiDAR (Mid-360) with SLAM pose; simulation uses RGB-D + pose
setting.action_space: frontier goals passed to A*/local planner producing continuous velocity commands (simulation: Habitat discrete steps)
setting.simulator: Habitat (HM3D, MP3D, HM3D-OVON, TextNav) plus real world

Efficiency figures (task time 21.5 s online / 27.8 s offline, on the first 100 HM3D episodes) are not in the numbers list.
results: HiCo-Nav reaches SR/SPL of 48.5/21.5 on MP3D (vs. WMNav 45.4/17.2), 61.0/31.8 on HM3D (best SR; ApexNav 59.6/33.0), 52.4/20.7 on HM3D-OVON (vs. TANGO 35.5/19.5) and 27.8/12.9 on TextNav (vs. UniGoal 20.2/11.4). It completes tasks in 21.5 s at real-time speed on a Jetson Orin NX-equipped quadruped.
limitations: Relies on a 2D exploration map, so it cannot handle cross-floor targets (13.9% of MP3D and 18.5% of HM3D episodes fail this way).

False positives from dataset annotation errors and perception errors under difficult viewpoints, and step-limit failures in large scenes; small objects in the real world are only 65% successful due to motion blur.
Depends on external VLM API calls (Qwen3-Omni) for the main real-world results, and there is no evaluation on instruction-following VLN benchmarks such as R2R.
